senses: A measure of the strength of an explosion or a bomb based on how many thousand tons of TNT would be needed to produce the same energy. (A derived unit for TNT equivalent.)
One thousand short tons (10³ × 2000 lb).
One thousand long tons (10³ × 2240 lb).
One thousand metric tons (10³ × 2204.6 lb).
ety: From kilo- + ton.
examples: That's a 300-kiloton nuclear warhead.
Halifax in Canada was devastated by a ship exploding in 1917. SS Mont Blanc, a French vessel loaded with 2.9 kilotons of explosives, collided with the Imo.

senses: To deform under stress.
ety: Attested since 1788. Origin unknown. Possibly related to Spanish chapuzar (“to sink by the head”).
examples: There are even cases where a totally different knot may result when carelessly pulled. Tie the Granny Knot around any object and pull one end, and it will capsize into Two Half Hitches.

senses: The science of cosmetics.
The profession of a cosmetologist or beautician.
ety: From French cosmétologie. By surface analysis, cosmetics + -ology.
examples: While still in high school, Mr. Niami took night classes to get his cosmetology license, then learned how to do special-effects prosthetics for horror films.

senses: Work, especially research or preparation, that involves significant walking, travel, or similar effort.
Skillful or vigorous use of the legs, as in dance or sports.
ety: From leg + work.
examples: John did all the legwork. He had the invitations printed and mailed. He found speakers.
Fancy legwork and jumping rope will get you in great shape.

senses: A craftsman who has knowledge of a manufacturing secret (specifically in the area of porcelain manufacturing).
A person who studies arcana or religious mysteries.
ety: From arcane + -ist; in the sense of a craftsman with secret knowledge about porcelain manufacturing, borrowed from German Arcanist.
examples: Ringler has the merit of having raised himself from a common potter to an “Arcanist,” as the Germans term one who is the sole depositor of an important secret;

senses: The grass Chrysopogon zizanioides (synonym Vetiveria zizanioides), which is native to India, but planted throughout the tropics for its fragrant roots and for erosion control.
The aromatic root of the grass.
An essential oil derived from the root; the fragrance of the oil.
ety: From French vétyver (older spelling) or vétiver, from Tamil வெட்டிவேர் (veṭṭivēr).
examples: Two types of vetiver have been found in India – (i) flowering or seeding vetiver which grows wild in North India, and (ii) non-flowering or non-seeding vetiver which is cultivated in South India.
She pressed his hand and was gone in a mist of vetiver, abruptly as the other evening.
Essential oils such as jasmine, rose, vetiver, ilang-ilang, iris, vanilla, sandalwood or lavender cannot be synthesised in the laboratory.

senses: Any of several passerine birds of the genera Quiscalus, Hypopyrrhus, Lampropsar and Macroagelaius, of the Americas, having iridescent plumage.
ety: From translingual Gracula, from Latin graculus (“jackdaw”).
examples: Outside, a gang of grackles combed the landscaped lawn like a homicide squad dragging a field for evidence.

senses: A mournful poem or piece of music composed or performed as a memorial to a deceased person.
A song or piece of music that is considered too slow, bland or boring.
ety: From Middle English dirige, from Latin dirige (“steer, direct”), from the beginning of the first antiphon in matins for the dead, Dirige, Domine, deus meus, in conspectu tuo viam meam. Doublet of dirige.
examples: It was as if the night sang dirges with clenched teeth.
Over six sections – a prologue, a life-story, a dream-quest, a dirge, a masque and an epilogue – they meditate on their lives, their hopes, their losses, and on the human condition.

senses: A horse chestnut, used in the game of conkers.
ety: As a term for horse chestnut, derived from the name of the game conkers, which came first. Theories for the original meaning include 19th-century dialect conker (“snail-shell”) (the game of conkers was originally played using snail-shells), from conch + -er, or a variant of conquer.
examples: His bald spot gleams like a burnished conker.

Unboxing conkers? What on earth are you talking about? Oh wow, you really are out of the loop, aren’t you? Gen Zers are taking to TikTok to film themselves unpeeling conkers from their spiky capsules.

senses: To turn into a demon.
To describe or represent as evil or diabolic, usually falsely.
ety: From Medieval Latin daemonizō, from daemon + -izō. Compare Ancient Greek δαιμονίζομαι (daimonízomai, “to be possessed by a demon”), from δαίμων (daímōn, “demon”). By surface analysis, demon + -ize.
examples: He calls for a “massive, urgent recruitment effort,” which is a fine idea, but one that’s likely to be futile unless we stop demonizing teachers and start paying them fairly.
It brags “we can replace them”—and gaslights and demonizes those who notice and object to being replaced.

senses: A scene in an opera.
An accompanied dramatic recitative, interspersed with passages of melody, or followed by a full aria.
The stage of an ancient theatre.
ety: Borrowed from Italian scena. Doublet of scene.
examples: Few Contralto singers are unacquainted with the beautiful Scena, Ah rendimi qual core, from Mitrane.

senses: Expressive of or pertaining to attitude.
ety: From Italian attitudine + -al, from Latin aptitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin aptitūdō, from aptus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, attitude + -al.
examples: While Noice is generally positive about the police department he thinks that there are attitudinal problems among some of the rank and file.

senses: Of or characterized by straps.
ety: From strap + -y.
examples: The click-click-click of strappy stilettos has given way to the clomp-clomp-clomp of platforms and wedges on the Milan catwalk.
We read newspaper accounts of the Reagans' black-tie evenings, where the women wore long, shimmering gowns and strappy high heels and everyone toasted equally elegant foreign guests.

senses: Resembling or characteristic of a rat; ratlike.
Infested with rats.
In poor condition or repair.
Crazy, mad; ridiculous; slightly strange, eccentric; also (followed by about, on, or over), attracted to, infatuated with.
Annoyed, bad-tempered, irritable.
ety: From rat + -y (suffix meaning ‘having the quality of’ forming adjective).
examples: The Marcher lord was still clad in his ratty black cloak and dented breastplate with its chipped enamel lightning.
I was having exactly that thought on a ratty mock-leather couch in Islington.
He got bad, he got ratty, he would take it out on people around him. He was mean when it turned against him.

senses: Government by elders; government by elderly rulers.
ety: From geronto- + -cracy, from Ancient Greek.
examples: It would come as no surprise to find that optimum science policy is apt to be developed neither by gerontocracy nor by juvenocracy but, like the community of scientists itself, by age-diversified meritocracy.
Young people who are close to writing off the Democratic Party as a dinosaur, as a gerontocracy of prudish abuelos who gave birth by immaculate conception, may be in for a pleasant surprise.

senses: Somewhat mad or eccentric.
ety: From daff + -y.
examples: Now I'm hungry as a Rocky Mountain lion so come, let's go and get this poor, daffy, tealess widow and wine and dine with her and make it all up.
He was daffy about her and she could twist him around her little finger.

senses: White, whitish, or greyish-white.
White or grey with age.
Old or old-fashioned; trite.
ety: Possibly from Middle English *hori (suggested by horilocket (“hoary-locked, having hoary locks or curls”)), equivalent to hoar + -y. Alternatively, Middle English horilocket may represent Middle English hor (“hoar, hoary”) + ilocket (“locked”) rather than hori (“hoary”) + locket (“locked”).
examples: But hoary Winter, unadorn'd and bare, Dwells in the dire Retreat, and freezes there.
The old man bowed his hoary head in acquiescence.
And ever and anon a silent tear Stole down, and trickled from his hoary beard.

senses: Any of several machines or devices in which a part impacts on another, or on a material.
An object which impacts another.
ety: Borrowed from New Latin impāctor, from impingō + -tor.
examples: Although Dr. Bottke remains unconvinced that the impactor had a cometary origin, he noted that the asteroid explanation also raised many exciting and unresolved questions.

senses: To make operational.
To define (a concept) in such a way that it can be practically measured.
ety: From operational + -ize.
examples: I have a lot of sexual fantasies that I'm never going to operationalize. I enjoy them just as fantasies.
To operationalize a concept is to identify those variables in terms of which the phenomenon represented by the concept can be accurately observed.
Vision seems ‘childishly simple’ to us but proves to be fiendishly hard to operationalise, precisely because we are so good at it.

senses: Good-natured banter; raillery.
Frivolous, lighthearted discussion of a topic.
ety: From French persiflage, from persifler (“to quiz, tease, mock”), from per- + siffler (“to whistle”), from Latin sībilō (“whistle”).
examples: After the third strike he returned to the bench to face the inevitable persiflage from his teammates.
Polite dinner calls for persiflage rather than in-depth possibly offensive discussion.

senses: Any of a group of burrowing amphibians of the order Gymnophiona that resemble earthworms or snakes.
ety: From Latin caecilia + -an, feminine form of Caecilius, from Caeculus + -ius, from caecus + -ulus.
examples: Today we have just three major lineages of amphibians - the anurans (frogs and toads), the newts and salamanders, and the worm-like caecilians, all of which can trace their ancestry back to long before the dinosaurs.

senses: Any lizard in the infraorder Gekkota.
Any lizard of the family Gekkonidae of small, carnivorous, mostly nocturnal animals with large eyes and adhesive toes enabling them to climb on vertical and upside-down surfaces.
ety: The modern form was probably borrowed into English and other European languages from Dutch gekko (1718). Contemporary English forms were chacco (1711) and jackoa (1724). The further origin is not quite clear. Some sources mention a supposed Malay gekok, gekoq, or gekop, which would be imitative of the gecko’s chirping sound. Another theory derives it from Acehnese gèh-gòh (“busy”).
examples: Leishmania infantum in Experimental Animals.—Experiments were carried out with geckoes, white mice, field mice (Microtus güntheri) and hamsters (Cricetus auratus and Cricetulus griseus).
The potential uses for gecko-inspired adhesive products are nearly endless. People have found possible uses for them from sports and robotics, to medicine and home improvement.

senses: The act of inhabiting; state of inhabiting or dwelling, or of being inhabited; occupancy.
A place of abode; settled dwelling; residence; house.
A group, lodge, or company, as of the Primrose League.
ety: From Middle English habitacioun, from Old French habitacion, abitacion (“act of dwelling”), from Latin habitātiōnem, accusative of Latin habitātiō.
examples: The few miserable hovels that shewed some marks of human habitation, were now of still rarer occurrence; and, at length, as we began to ascend a huge and uninterrupted swell of moorland, they totally disappeared.
Now, however, the windows in the houses began one by one to be lit up, giving a greater sense of habitation and humanity.
And as imagination bodies forth The forms of things unknown, the poet’s pen Turns them to shapes and gives to airy nothing A local habitation and a name.

senses: Any Moorish fortress in Spain.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish alcázar, from Arabic الْقَصْر (al-qaṣr). Doublet of castle.
examples: But most eloquent of all were the stories passed down to her - highly decorated items which Harriet embellished even further in her resolute myth of the enchanted alcazar, the fairy chateau that never was.

senses: A piece of broken glass or pottery, especially one found in an archaeological dig.
A piece of material, especially rock and similar materials, reminding of a broken piece of glass or pottery.
A food preparation similar in shape to a shard of, e.g., glass, generally made from a sheet of a hard product that is then shattered to produce smaller pieces.
A tough scale, sheath, or shell; especially an elytron of a beetle.
An instance of an MMORPG that is one of several independent and structurally identical virtual worlds, none of which has so many players as to exhaust a system's resources.
ety: From Middle English shard, scherd, scheard, schord, from Old English sċeard (“a broken piece; shard”), from Proto-West Germanic *skard, from Proto-Germanic *skardą (“notch; nick”), from *skardaz (“damaged; nicked; scarred”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”). Akin to Scots schaird (“shard”), French écharde (“splinter”), Dutch schaarde (“tear; notch; fragment”), German Scharte (“notch”), Old Norse skarð (“notch, hack”) ( > Danish skår). The database sense is perhaps derived from the online gaming sense or from SHARD (System for Highly Available Replicated Data), name of a 1980s datab
examples: You know there is something fascinating beyond that wall because someone's tried to stop you seeing over, and there are shards of glass embedded in the top.
A shard of chocolate adorns the dish.

senses: Absence from school or work; truancy.
ety: First attested in 1848 in New York City. Most likely from Dutch hoekje (“nook, corner; 'spot to hide' in hide-and-seek”). Formerly, "hoekje spelen" could be used to mean "to play hide-and-seek", though the common term for the game nowadays is verstoppertje. By surface analysis, hook + -y.
examples: Let's play hooky and go to the mall.

I was already two years late getting to college. I was twenty, not eighteen like most people who were about to graduate. All that hooky playing, stealing, and getting sent to juvenile jails had set me way back.

senses: A person who is knowledgeable of, or who collects antiques (especially one holding an official position); an antiquarian.
An aficionado or student of antiquities, ancient artifacts, historic sites, ancient writings, or relics of the past.
ety: From Latin antīquārius (“pertaining to antiquity, one fond of or employed in antiquities”), from antīquus (“ancient”) + -ārius; equivalent to antique + -ary.
examples: The sound of the bubbling water grew more distinct, as the ear became accustomed to its music: it reminded him of one very like it in Etheringhame Park. Both might have made the delight of either antiquary or poet.

senses: The state of being a serf.
The feudal system that includes serfs.
ety: From serf + -dom.
examples: Krzywicki's studies of primitive societies led him to conclude that there was no universal law and that, for example, serfdom was not a necessary stage in all cases.

senses: To reject the truth or validity of; to deny.
To refuse to have any relation to; to disown.
To refuse to pay or honor (a debt).
To be repudiated.
ety: First attested in 1543; from Latin repudiātus, the perfect passive participle of repudiō (“to cast off, reject”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)), from repudium (“rejection, repudiation, divorce”).
examples: The fierce willingness to repudiate domination in a holistic manner is the starting point for progressive cultural revolution.
If a man like Malcolm X could change and repudiate racism, if I myself and other former Muslims can change, if young whites can change, then there is hope for America.

senses: A ghost or phantom.
A scare or fright.
A metaphysical manifestation; an artificial distinction or construct.
ety: Borrowed from Dutch spook (“ghost”), from Middle Dutch spooc (“spook, ghost”). Cognate with Middle Low German spôk, spûk (“apparition, ghost”), Middle High German gespük (“a haunting”), German Spuk, Danish spøge (“to haunt”), Swedish spöke (“ghost”).
examples: The building was haunted by a couple of spooks.
The big spider gave me a spook.
He who is infatuated with Man leaves persons out of account so far as that infatuation extends, and floats in an ideal, sacred interest. Man, you see, is not a person, but an ideal, a spook.

senses: The state of being a peon; the system of paying back debt through servitude and labour; loosely, any system of involuntary servitude.
ety: From peon + -age.
examples: But there was work to be done down in the Salinas Valley where César Chávez was organizing the grape pickers and lettuce workers out of their state of un-unionized peonage.

senses: The great white shark (Carcharodon carcharias).
ety: Borrowed from French requin (“shark”).
examples: The big gullet of the requin shark, for example, could do so. It has been killed with men inside whole.

senses: The Japanese art of crocheting or knitting stuffed yarn toys, typically creatures having oversized heads.
Such a stuffed toy crocheted or knitted from yarn.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 編み包み (amigurumi), a blend of 編む (amu, “to knit”) + 縫い包み (nuigurumi, “stuffed toy”).
examples: And since most amigurumi tends to be on the small side, you will use these small diameter circular knitting techniques frequently.

senses: Of a person, having eyes filled with tears; inclined to cry.
Of eyes, filled with tears.
ety: From Middle English tery; equivalent to tear + -y.
examples: No wonder Ryan was teary; he missed his parents.
Wade looked into his girlfriend's teary eyes.

senses: A person who lives near two coasts.
ety: From bi- + coastal.
examples: Ms. Zohn said being married bicoastals poses a variety of challenges, not the least of which is explaining their situation.

senses: The act of seizing for public use; impressing into public service, especially military service and (most often) naval service.
ety: From impress + -ment.
examples: A month later the governors of six more states, meeting in conference, enigmatically urged the impressment of slaves for “the public service as may be required.”

senses: Anything that is particularly good of its class.
A very good-looking person.
ety: From belt (“hit”) + -er (agent noun suffix).
examples: When the second goal came, it was a belter - Fabregas launching an inch-perfect ball over the top for Van Persie to volley in without breaking stride.

senses: A refreshing drink flavored with aromatic herbs, especially mint, and sometimes alcohol.
ety: From Middle English, from Old French julep, from Medieval Latin julapium, via Arabic جُلَاب (julāb) from Persian گلاب (golâb, “rosewater”), from گل (“rose”) + آب (“water”).
examples: He wouldnt even let old Wilkie touch it do you remember Gerald but always gathered it himself and made his own julep. He was as crochety about his julep as an old maid, measuring everything by a recipe in his head.
Yo, we be making mountains out of Cool Whip / Pass me the mint for the julep
In 1797 the American Museum described the Virginian who upon rising “drinks a julep made of rum, water, and sugar, but very strong.” The mint was added a few years later.

senses: A female leader of a family, a tribe or an ethnic or religious group.
The dominant female in a family group of elephants.
A strong and domineering older woman; a battle axe.
A female founder of a political or religious movement, an organization or an enterprise.
ety: Of Latin origin, via or reinforced by Old French matriarche, from Latin māter (“mother”) + -archa, -arches, from Ancient Greek -άρχης (-árkhēs), from ἀρχός (arkhós, “chief”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ergʰ- (“to begin, rule, command”). By surface analysis, matri- + -arch.
examples: This female hyena also gets erections and is larger, more aggressive than the male hyenas and lives in matrilineal clans of up to 80 individuals governed by an alpha female matriarch.

senses: A large carton that fits on a pallet, used for transporting goods.
ety: Genericized trademark of the Gaylord Container Corporation, a manufacturer of packaging materials, itself from the surname Gaylord.
examples: They come sorted according to type, in large cardboard gaylord boxes (you'll see pumpkins in these containers at supermarkets) or shrink-wrapped on a pallet.
